summary: Circular metal tower at the end of Muskegon's south pier, lit 1903; pier lights since 1872; the 1919 steamer wreck and keepers' rescues; tower open on summer tours.

lens.where: removed to the 1903 tower from the land-based lighthouse

structures.note: Circular metal tower near the inner end of the south pier; LighthouseFriends calls it circular and metal, Muskegon Lights calls it a tower open for summer tours.
The first Muskegon light, on the south side of the river. Not the pier light.
Fixed red light with a fog bell; removed after 1903.
Frame building at the outer end of the south pier, with a ten-inch steam whistle.

access.note: Pier and breakwater walkable; the Coast Guard and NOAA facilities are at the shore end of the pier. Tower open on docent-led summer tours.

events.note: Land-based dwelling with wooden tower on the south side of the river (not the pier light)
Dwelling with square tower and fourth-order lens completed
Wooden pierhead tower at the outer end of the south pier: fixed red light, sixth order, fog bell
Post light on the end of the south pier forms a range with the wooden tower; fog bell in operation 366 hours in the fiscal year ended 30 June 1891

corrections.why: The record's tower (cast iron, conical, pier) was built in 1903 (USLHS 'Year Tower Established: 1903'; LighthouseFriends). The 1851 date belongs to the first, land-based Muskegon light on the south side of the river.

The record's 10.4 m (34 ft) does not match the USLHS place record's light height (53 ft, 16.2 m) as far as the cached page shows. Check the USLHS figure against the 1903 Light List before changing it.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's 1851 date and 'cast iron' tower describe different structures: the 1851 light was a land-based dwelling with a wooden tower, and the cast-iron pier tower was built in 1903 (USLHS; LighthouseFriends).

notes_for_editor: Roster matched to the USLHS place by name and position (0.47 km). The roster starts in 1895 and is printed verbatim; LighthouseFriends gives the keepers from 1851 to 1894, which are added as LighthouseFriends-only lines. The NRHP nomination PDF is a not-digitised placeholder; the 2006 listing comes from the NPGallery asset record. Identity: the USLHS record for 'Muskegon South Pierhead' gives 'Muskegon South Pierhead Range Rear' as an alternate name. The Board and Bulletin call the station 'Muskegon Pierhead range' or 'Muskegon Pierhead Light and Fog Signal Station'; the keepers named in the Bulletins match this station's roster. The Board's 1894 conduit is for the 'Muskegon Pierhead range, front' light; the story calls it the front light of the range and does not identify it with the 1903 tower. The Board's 1891 'Muskegon Pierhead' fog bell (366 hours) is taken as this pier's bell on the basis of LighthouseFriends' 1872 fog bell; the Board does not say which pier, and the story says the attribution is probable, not certain. Conflicts: (1) Wikipedia-style leads say the first Muskegon light was brick; LighthouseFriends says rubblestone. Not cited. (2) The 1919 ship: the Bulletin says steamer Muskegon; LighthouseFriends says City of Muskegon. (3) The death toll (15 of 37 passengers, 7 crew) is from LighthouseFriends only; the Bulletin gives no count and the Chronicling America search for 1919 returned nothing usable. Check against a 1919 newspaper before printing the number. (4) The tower's lens versus lantern: LighthouseFriends says the 1903 tower took the fourth-order lens from the land-based light; a lead source says it reused the 1870 lantern room. (5) Focal height and tower height in the record (10.4 m; 14.5 m) do not match the USLHS record (53 ft focal; 30 ft tower). The Bulletin OCR for the 1919 wreck is column-interleaved, so the story quotes only the contiguous phrases ('the fog signal and then went to the wreck'; the commendation sentence on p. 51). The 1913, 1914, 1915 and 1917 quotes are checked against the PDF text. Access: Michigan Lighthouse Conservancy's visitor page covers both the pier and the breakwater lights; it is the only source for the summer schedule, so check it before going. Keepers named are historical; none is a living-person issue beyond the public role.
